So I've been looking at a ton of execution questions. A lot of the are like figure out why we are having a problem / decline in users... I usually don't have to ask a data scientist to tell me the problem in the real world... I guess my question is why ask this..
I like the goal setting / metric stuff because that actually makes sense... but I'd take any thoughts on this.

To clarify, we usually have metrics we want to live by, but the contrived solution like 'hey we lost like 10% DAU, you have to figure out the problem' is weird. I mean the issues are usually easily identifiable by data... But I can see they want to know your breadth of reasoning but just not something I deal with in that manner...
they want to see if you know what metrics to speak about, and how to lean on resources in the organization (in my opinion)
if you go "what's a DAU" or "I don't know" that's a clear signal
i hate hypothetical open ended questions in general
they're 10X harder than the actual job
where you'll have numbers and people to speak to about issues

Hmm. Well usually when something like that happened, people come up with the issue and look for a solution. I’m not ‘interviewing an analyst’ to find out what he knows. Sure they look to us for a solution or best path forward. But I guess them wanting to know if we know what the org cares about is a legit question.
I appreciate the input, thank you!

As a PM you need to have "strong opinions, but weakly held" to figure out different solutions, iterate and experiment on them, etc. 
If you as the PM don't have good hypothesis on why user engagement is low, then the team will be without direction. It's also often not one thing, but the intent is to find out if you can consider a variety of things to get to the real problem.

user decline is a valid scenario it need not be tracked at org level only but at individual feature that you are working might contribute to this decline. so as a TPM how do you find that out ..you can take help of Analytics but sometime they take few days to analyze and come back with the data but  is there a quick way to find out ..say if your feature, after it went live started causing more decline then how do you identify this quickly so you can fix forward or rollback the changes, you will use kibana/grafana or splunk dashboard to quickly identify the root cause and act accordingly. As a TPM you should be on top of this and this is what interviewer is trying to asses.

Any thoughts on what's "too soon" for switching companies?
From personal perspective or professional perspective?
both

I think personally if you know it’s not a right fit there is no obligation to stick around. You don’t own anyone anything. The company that you are at is paying you to do the job, and if you quit they no longer have to pay you… simple as that.

From a future employer (professional perspective) I think they want to know why when it comes to a jump so soon in a company. That decision process could be a benefit. But I would say that less than 2-3 months is probably a red flag (without a good story!)

I have seen so many examples. People accepting a job but it not really being what they actually signed up for, accepting a job offer from company A but then later getting an offer from company B, having to move for family reasons shortly after accepting a new role. Again it just kind of depends. But whatever you do - trust yourself and put yourself first.
I think moving to another company in less than 1.5 year is "too soon" but if the role is not right for you, and you're not showing a pattern in your resume it's ok!!
Agreed! I think the bigger picture is a pattern forming. If it happens once it ok. If it happens 6 times there’s a trend.

Do you mean TPM managers building a team a team of TPMs from scratch? I have done a lot of 0-1 and actually enjoy it - be it managing programs as initial TPM on team/org or building a team. Reasons - opportunity to set a culture, bring about efficiencies that didn't exist etc.
Do Tpm ever  build the Eng team
Yup, I mean standing up a TPM function from scratch or inheriting/scaling an existing team

Each model offers something  different for a “0-1” builder vs. a “scaler” builder. My theory is that there are leader archetypes mapping to each and then I believe a generalist who can do both. I also doubt career expectations matrices take into account the different skill sets needed to scale from scratch vs the culture dev/carrier work needed from a leader who scales

Finally, I suspect  0-1 archetypes skew towards entrepreneurial vs scalers who may have superior relationship building/political skills. If I were building out a long-term TPM function, or expanding my TPM mgr bench, I’d bring in the 0-1 archetype to establish a foundation until the team in question was ready to fully norm, then a scaler to norm/scale the team. But are people aware of these archetypes? Do TPM leaders hiring mgrs on their teams agree that they may exist? Just random thoughts that touch on org design, archetypes, and team development..

All good questions. I would argue that one has to adapt so you can start of as the builder but you have to know how to scale and be ready for it. You need both skills for long term success. Good TPM leaders would know what they need in the next manager even if they may not use the same terms

I've had the full range of experiences here: building from a 0 base, taking over teams when the leader had moved to a different opportunity, losing and gaining teams in reorgs, etc. 
1/ there's ofcoz nothing better than building from the ground up. You hire the people you want and structure it the way you want as well. 
2/ having said that you can't choose what hand you get dealt, especially at a place like FB where there's a reorg every 3 mos, leadership vacuum gets created when people move into other teams/companies, etc. There have been times when I've said yes to a new opportunity and that has opened so many doors, but also other times when I've regretted saying yes due to org politics etc. in the new role. 

The harder path is when your boss leaves, and suddenly you are expected to lead the full team, but also manage people who were till the day before, your peers. Again, have had good experiences with mature people understanding the move and people who wanted the manager job leaving cuz they didn't get it. 
In hindsight, all of these experiences make you who you are and I'm thankful for then. If you follow a good core set of first principles, it makes all of this a tad bit easier, IMHO.

Hello, Anyone preparing for AWS Solution Architect Associate certification or have done it recently? Any tips you can share. Preparing for it if anyone is interested, we can form study group

I recently renewed my solution architect cert. Below are some tips:
1. Schedule your exam so that you are working towards a target (give atleast a month or two to prepare)
2. Pick a course from Udemy (Stephen marrek, neal davis, zeal vora’s courses are good). 
3. Do all the hands on exercises. I know ppl who cleared without doing hands on but personally I enjoy playing with technology and doing hands on made me more confident in my responses
4. Start with mock tests atleast 2 weeks prior to actual test. AWS solution architect questions are scenario based and verbose so this will help develop habit of reading long questions and find most relevant response (there can be more than 1 correct response you need to select most relevant)
5. Review your test responses- correct as well as incorrect to validate your understanding. This will also highlight areas that need more practice, and you can revisit those sections.
6. If you are consistently scoring > 80% you are good to proceed with the test.

AWS allows 3 reschedules if you do it 24 hours in advance.  DM me if you have any other questions.

Getting few DMs so editing  to include mock test recommendation : Udemy has neal davis, and stephen mareek’s mock test courses sold separately, tutorial dojo by jon bonso is considered very good too.

We should discuss this topic in detail. I am in the same boat. Transitioned from software Eng to tpm. Now I don’t see much growth on tpm side but at the same time, I find it difficult to go back to engineering side as I am not doing hands on for last 5 years. 

What are the options for me? What can I do to try other options. 
1) Move back as an engineering manager - I saw few people in this role with TPM background, can they survive without hands on? Is there anyone who tried this.
2) Transition to Product - Few colleagues in my current company suggested to join as a product manager but I need to accept role one level below. I didn’t like this idea as I will be starting again as a junior product manager.
3) Solution Architect - What is the future for this role? Is it safe? What skills are needed?

I think you have a future with all pathways.  
1 - I like to think you'll be an excellent EM having the mixed bag of experience that you have.  Also, unless you're at Google or maybe Apple, you won't be doing coding much as an EM.  So this pathway is very much open to you.  I could be considered in the same situation with a past both technical and TPM roles.  So now you know 1 who has done this.
2 - Transitioning to Product is also an option and one that would probably the least resistance to what you are currently doing. I don't know that you'll have much better opportunities at growth though over what you have currently.
3 - There's likely always going to be a future for Solution Architects.  Systems NEED architecting and having that deeper technical understanding is key.  Skills needed are heavy in the system design area, but also hands on.  I would say the skill level is very high technically though so if you're light on this because of your past 5 years this is probably the most difficult move.
